name: gnu-prolog
why: A real Prolog compiler with finite-domain constraint solving is an old-school logic language worth a long afternoon of puzzles.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Prolog is a free Prolog compiler with a finite-domain (FD) constraint solver, developed by Daniel Diaz. It takes Prolog and constraint programs and compiles them to stand-alone native binaries, similar to how gcc turns C source into an executable. It also ships an interactive top-level interpreter with a debugger, and the gprolog, gplc and related tools are its command-line front ends. The homepage describes the Prolog part as ISO-conformant with many extensions such as global variables, DCGs, sockets and OS interface.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it as a way to combine the power of constraint programming with the declarativity of logic programming, in a free, native-code system. It was inspired by the author's earlier systems wamcc (Prolog to C via the WAM, slowed by gcc compile times) and clp(FD) (a single-primitive FD constraint design), and development began in January 1996 under the name Calypso.
brief.how_it_works: The compiler is based on the Warren Abstract Machine. A Prolog program is first compiled to a WAM file, then translated to a machine-independent low-level language called mini-assembly, then to the target machine's assembly, and finally to a native object and executable. Unused built-in predicates are excluded at link time, which keeps executables small. The FD solver defines all high-level constraints in terms of a single low-level primitive, which the homepage says makes constraints compilable and lets users define their own.

commands_seen.context: From the Reporting Bugs section: the homepage asks bug reporters to run this to report the GNU Prolog version.
From the Reporting Bugs section: suggested Unix command for reporting the machine type in a bug report. It is a general shell command, not a GNU Prolog one.

brief.install_notes: The homepage offers a source tarball (gprolog-1.5.0.tar.gz) and mentions a configure step, since bug reports should include the operands given to configure and its output. Binary options are a Mac OS X installer package made with MacPorts (installs to /opt/local/ and /opt/local/bin), and Windows 32-bit and 64-bit auto-install setups built with MSVC++ or MinGW. Windows builds are also described in src/WINDOWS and src/WINDOWS-OLD inside the source tree. The page does not mention Homebrew specifically, so the brew formula details are not confirmed here. Notepad++ users can import a UDL file for syntax highlighting.
brief.standout: Native-code output for a Prolog system, with the FD solver built on one primitive that users can extend, plus a claimed performance comparable to commercial solvers. Its compiler design avoids gcc's compile-time cost by generating assembly directly.
brief.status: Appears maintained but the homepage shows no release date. It lists gprolog-1.5.0 as the current stable version and has a copyright line of 1999-2021. The page also mentions a GIT repository on GitHub and separate unstable and old-version directories. Last release date and last commit are unknown from this page alone.
brief.caveats: Platform support is broad but varies: Linux, BSDs, Solaris, macOS and Windows (Cygwin, MinGW, MinGW64, MSVC++) on x86, plus ARM, PowerPC, SPARC, alpha and MIPS entries that may be older. The homepage does not give a licence name, only that it is free software. The homepage's own macOS binary was built on Big Sur, so newer macOS may depend on a source build. Windows builds have separate instructions in the source tree. The manual is available in many formats, but I did not open it.
quotes: GNU Prolog is a free Prolog compiler with constraint solving over finite domains developed by Daniel Diaz.
GNU Prolog accepts Prolog+constraint programs and produces native binaries (like gcc does from a C source).
The key feature of the GNU Prolog solver is the use of a single (low-level) primitive to define all (high-level) FD constraints.
